title: Choose Your Novel
learn: Learn how to choose a just-right book and why reading self-chosen texts helps you grow as a reader.
summary: A just-right book is one you can read mostly on your own. You understand most words, meet a few new ones, and want to keep reading. Try one page: if more than about five words stop you, the book may be too hard right now. If every word is effortless, it may be too easy. Choose a book that gives you a manageable challenge.

title: Preview and Predict
learn: Use book clues to make and revise predictions.
summary: Before chapter one, readers preview the cover, title, back-cover summary, chapter titles, and opening pages. A prediction is a smart guess based on clues. It can change as you learn more.

title: Note-Taking and New Words
learn: Annotate reading and collect new vocabulary.
summary: Active readers leave a trail of thinking. Jot a reaction, question, important detail, or quick sketch as you read. Also collect unfamiliar words so you can use them later.

title: Vocabulary: Warming Up to New Words
learn: Use context clues to infer word meaning.
summary: Context clues are words and details around an unfamiliar word. A nearby definition, example, opposite, synonym, or the overall situation can help you make a strong meaning guess.

title: Meet the Main Character
learn: Analyze a protagonist's internal and external responses.
summary: The protagonist is the main character. Readers learn about characters through what they do and say on the outside and what they think or feel on the inside. Internal feelings often help explain external actions.

title: Who Is Telling the Story?
learn: Analyze narrator point of view.
summary: A narrator is the voice telling a story. First person uses I, me, and we because a character tells the story. Third person uses he, she, and they. A third-person narrator may know one character's thoughts or many characters' thoughts. Point of view controls what readers can know.

title: Where and When
learn: Analyze setting and visualize its effect.
summary: Setting is where and when a story happens. Place, time period, traditions, rules, technology, and events can shape what characters can do. Readers turn descriptions into a mental picture.

title: Naming the Genre
learn: Identify genre using text features.
summary: Genre is a category of story. Realistic fiction could happen in the real world. Fantasy includes magic or impossible worlds. Science fiction often includes future settings or advanced technology. Historical fiction is set in a real past. Genre features help readers know what to expect.

title: Vocabulary: Context Clues and a Dictionary Check
learn: Use context then verify meaning with a reference source.
summary: Use context clues to make a first guess about an unfamiliar word. Then check a dictionary or other reliable reference source. Compare the meaning you predicted with the meaning that fits the sentence.

title: Prove It with Evidence
learn: Make an inference and support it with evidence.
summary: An inference is a logical conclusion based on clues in a text and what you already know. Textual evidence is the specific word, action, quotation, or detail that proves your idea comes from the book.

title: How the Parts Build the Whole
learn: Analyze how a scene or chapter contributes to structure.
summary: A chapter or scene has a job in the whole story. It may move the plot, deepen a character, reveal information, build tension, or develop a mood. Authors make structure choices such as chapter breaks, pacing, flashbacks, and cliffhangers.

title: When Reading Gets Confusing
learn: Monitor comprehension and use fix-up strategies.
summary: Strong readers notice when meaning breaks down. They repair understanding by rereading, slowing down, looking back, asking a question, using context clues, or checking a reference source.

title: Figurative Language
learn: Interpret figurative language and its effect.
summary: Figurative language is not meant literally. A simile compares using like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human traits to something nonhuman. Authors use figurative language to create images, emotions, and ideas.

title: Voice and Mood
learn: Analyze how word choice creates voice and mood.
summary: Voice is the personality that comes through in a narrator's or character's words, sentence patterns, and attitude. Mood is the feeling a scene creates for readers. Authors build both through specific language and details.

title: Vocabulary: Cracking Words into Parts
learn: Use roots, prefixes, and suffixes with context clues.
summary: Many words contain meaningful parts. A prefix comes before a root, a root carries core meaning, and a suffix comes after it. Use word parts and context clues together to make a strong meaning prediction.

title: The Turning Point
learn: Identify the main tension event of your novel and explain its importance.
summary: The story's high point of tension is when the main conflict reaches a turning point. Earlier events build toward it through rising action. Afterward, the story moves toward resolution.

title: Choosing the Details That Matter
learn: Distinguish key details from minor details.
summary: Readers decide which details carry the most meaning. Key details reveal an important event, motivation, problem, change, or theme. Minor details may add interest but do not change understanding as much.

title: Reading Between the Lines
learn: Infer implicit meaning using textual clues.
summary: Explicit meaning is stated directly. Implicit meaning is suggested but not said. Readers infer implicit meaning by combining dialogue, actions, descriptions, and other clues.

title: Vocabulary: Words with Feelings
learn: Analyze connotation and shades of meaning.
summary: Words with similar dictionary meanings can carry different feelings. Connotation is the positive, negative, or neutral feeling a word suggests. Authors choose words carefully to guide readers' reactions.

title: Theme and Your Connection
learn: Determine theme with evidence and make a connection.
summary: A topic is a subject such as courage or friendship. A theme is a full message about that topic. Themes are developed through events, character choices, dialogue, symbols, and repeated ideas.

title: What the Author Wants You to Take Away
learn: Analyze author purpose and message.
summary: Authors write to entertain, inform, persuade, make readers feel, or invite readers to think differently. Their purpose and message are revealed through events, characters, structure, and language.

title: Step Into the Author's Chair
learn: Create an original scene using author craft.
summary: Writing in a novel's world means using what you know about its characters, setting, conflict, and voice. You can create a missing scene, alternate moment, or what-if scene while making it sound believable.

title: Your Honest, Updated Opinion
learn: Respond thoughtfully using reasons and evidence.
summary: A thoughtful book response includes a clear opinion, specific reasons, and evidence. Strong readers also revise their thinking when new events or evidence change their view.
